Accepted29JUN2020 tionship between orogenic growth and global climate and environment change (Aitchison et al., 2007;
Acceptedarticleonline2JUL2020 Chatterjee et al., 2013; Raymo & Ruddiman, 1992). Despite numerous methods that have been applied
(Huetal.,2016;Wuetal.,2014),thetimingoftheIndia‐Asiacollisionremainscontroversial,withestimates
rangingfrom~70Ma(Yin&Harrison,2000)to~34Ma(Aitchisonetal.,2007).Thediscrepanciesbetween
theseestimatesareattributednotonlytodifferentprecollisionallocationsbutalsotovariablegeometriesof
theAsiansouthernmarginpriortoIndia‐Asiacollision.
Paleomagnetismisoneofthemajormethodsthatcanbeusedforquantifyingplatepaleolatitudesandisthus
crucial for constraining the history of plate movement (Achache et al., 1984; Appel et al., 1998; Bian
et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2015; Liebke et al., 2010; Lippert et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2016;
Songetal.,2020;Sunetal.,2006;vanHinsbergenetal.,2012;Yang,Ma,Bian,etal.,2015;Yanetal.,2016).
Because the Lhasa terrane (LT) was located at the southern margin of Asia prior to India‐Asia collision
(Figure 1a), reliable Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the LT are essential to constrain the locations
and geometries of the precollisional margins of Asia. However, the published Cretaceous paleomagnetic
datasetsfrombothvolcanicandsedimentaryrocksyieldedawiderangeofinclinationsrangefrom17.7°
to41.9°, withthe consequence that the obtained paleolatitudesvary from9.9°N to26.7°N (Cao, Sun,Li,
et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2018; Pozzi et al., 1982; Sun et al., 2008, 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2013;
©2020.AmericanGeophysicalUnion.
AllRightsReserved. Tong et al., 2017; Yang, Ma, Zhang, et al., 2015; Yi et al., 2015). These conspicuous inconsistencies of

southern margin of Asia had a relatively east‐west alignment. However, after applying
syntectonic‐sedimentation correction, the Cretaceous paleomagnetic data from the LT indicated that the
precollisionalsouthernmarginofAsiamayhadaninvertedtriangleshape(Tongetal.,2019).Thelargeloca-
tionsandgeometriesdiscrepancyofprecollisionalsouthernmarginofAsiamaybeascribedtoseveralfac-
tors: (1) lower paleolatitudes observed from sedimentary strata may be partly attributed to
compaction‐induced inclination shallowing (Tauxe & Kent, 2004); (2) some volcanic paleomagnetic data
sets come from too limited lava flows to average secular variation (Achache et al., 1984); (3) the Late
CretaceousredbedssuchastheTakenaFormationorShexingFormationintheLinzhoubasinmayhave
sufferedfromremagnetization(Liangetal.,2017;Pozzietal.,1982);(4)theCretaceouspaleomagneticsam-
plesoftheLTwerecollectedfromtheunidentifiedsyntectonicgrowthstrata,whichleadtoinaccuratetilt
correctionforthepaleomagneticdata(Tongetal.,2019).
The Late Cretaceous strata in the LT mainly include sedimentary rocks, which can be divided into the
Takena Formation, Shexing Formation, and Jingzhushan Formation. These Late Cretaceous strata were
depositedindistinctareas,whichwereassignedtodifferentlocalnames,suchasGeji,Cuoqin,Nima,and
Linzhouareas.Structuralanalysisandregionalmappinghaveshownthat>50%north‐southcrustalshort-
eningtookplaceduringtheCretaceous(Kappetal.,2003;Volkmeretal.,2007),whichfurtherindicatedthat
east‐westtrendingfoldaxishasbeenwidelydevelopedintheLateCretaceousstrata.Mostofthepublished
LateCretaceouspaleomagneticdatasetsintheLTcomefromthesinglelimboffolds,whilepaleomagnetic
datasetsfromthetwolimbsoffoldsarerelativelyscarce(Tongetal.,2019).IftheseLateCretaceouspaleo-
magneticdataobtainedfromtheLTaredividedintotwogroups,theinclinationsfromthenorthernlimbof
folds(thesamplingstratadiptowardthenorth)areobviouslylowerthanthosefromthesouthernlimb(the
samplingstratadiptowardthesouth;Tongetal.,2019).TheEarlyCretaceouspaleomagneticdataalsodis-
played similar characteristics to the Late Cretaceous paleomagnetic data, in which the northern limbs
yielded a lower inclination than those of the southern limbs (Tong et al., 2019). Notably, the LT is long
andnarrow,extendingfor>2,000kmfromeasttowestand<300kmfromsouthtonorth.However,the
majority of the published Late Cretaceous sedimentary paleomagnetic data sets came from the Takena
Formation,ShexingFormation,andJingzhushanFormationinthecentral‐easternLT(Achacheetal.,1984;
Cao,Sun,Li,etal.,2017,Cao,Sun,Liu,etal.,2017;Pozzietal.,1982;Sunetal.,2012;Tongetal.,2017)and
onlyoneLateCretaceoussedimentarypaleomagneticresultderivedfromtheJingzhushanFormationinthe
westernLT(Yang,Ma,Zhang,etal.,2015).Therefore,high‐qualityCretaceouspaleomagneticdata,espe-
ciallythosefromthefarwesternLTandfromthetwolimbsoffoldsarestillurgentlyrequiredtoresolve
theissuesmentionedabove.
Inthispaper,wecarriedoutanewpaleomagneticinvestigationontheJingzhushanFormationredbedsin
theGejiareainthefarwesternLT.Ournewpaleomagneticresultsprovidedagreatopportunitytotestthe
inclinationdiscrepancyoftheLateCretaceouspaleomagneticdataintheLT.Besides,ournewpaleomag-
neticresultscanalsosignificantlycontributetorecoveringtheprecollisionalpaleogeographyoftheLT,as
wellasclarifyingtheprecollisionalgeometriesoftheAsiansouthernmargin.
2. Geological Background, Sampling, andLaboratory Procedures
TheTibetanPlateau,knownastheroofoftheworld,ismainlyregardedasacomplexagglomerationoffive
continentalfragmentsthatinclude,fromnorthtosouth,theKunlun‐Qaidam,Songpan‐Ganzi,Qiangtang,
Lhasa,andHimalayablocks(Figure1a).TheLTissandwichedbytheQiangtangterranetothenorthand
theTethyanHimalayatothesouth,withtheBangong‐NujiangsuturezoneandtheIndus‐Tsangposuture
zoneasboundaries.
Our studied area is located in the far western LT where Cretaceous volcanic and sedimentary rocks are
extensively exposed (Figure 1b). The Cretaceous strata mainly include, in ascending order, the
Jingzhushan,Langshan,Duoni,andQushenlaFormations.TheJingzhushanFormation,whichwasdepos-
itedangularly,unconformablyoverliestheLangshan,Duoni,andQushenlaFormations,andunderliesthe
NiubaoFormation.Itmainlyincludespurplish‐redsandstones,siltstones,andmudstones.Fossilsidentified
intheJingzhushanFormationincludeTylostomaferganense,Adiozoptyxiscf.coguandiana,indicativeofa
Late Cretaceous age (1:250,000 scale Geji County regional geological survey report (I44C004001), 2003).
Furthermore,theElectronSpinResonance(ESR)resultsandmagnetostratigraphicaldatingshowthatthe

bottomagesoftheJingzhushanFormationintheRituareaare~92.0±9.0Maand~96Ma,respectively(Li
etal.,2016).ThisageisgenerallyconsistentwiththeageoftheJingzhushanFormation(~92Ma)inthe
central northern LT as constrained by detrital zircon geochronology and micropaleontological data (Lai
et al., 2019). Besides, according to the presence of sporopollen assemblage (such as Coptosporites,
Leavigatosporites, Doltoidospora sp., Polypodiaceaesporites sp., Polypodiisporites sp., and Lygodiumsporites
sp.), the Jingzhushan Formation in the Nima area was assigned to the Late Cretaceous (Jia et al.,2007).
Lithofacies and sedimentary features suggest that the Jingzhushan Formation was deposited in an
alluvial‐fanandbraided‐riverenvironment(Laietal.,2019).

Generally,everypaleomagneticsiteincludesatleast10coresamplesandspansseveralmetersinastrati-
graphicthickness.Coresampleswerecollectedwithagasoline‐powereddrillandorientedusingbothmag-

Inordertoidentifymagneticcarriersandchoosetheproperdemagnetizationprocedure,theacquisitionof
isothermalremanentmagnetization(IRM),backfielddemagnetizationofsaturationIRM(SIRM),andther-
maldemagnetizationofthree‐axisIRMwereacquiredusinganASCIM10–30pulsemagnetizerandmea-
sured using a JR–6A spinner magnetometer on some representative samples. The three‐axis IRM
experiment successively imparted at 2.4 T, 0.4 T, and 0.12 T along the Z, Y, and X axes, respectively
(Lowrie,1990).Tofurtherestimatethecontributionsofdifferentmagneticminerals,IRMacquisitioncurves
wereanalyzedbasedoncumulativelog‐Gaussiananalysis(Kruiveretal.,2001).
Theanisotropyofmagneticsusceptibility(AMS)wasmeasuredatroomtemperatureusingaKLY–4bridge.
Allthestandardpaleomagneticspecimensweresubjectedtostepwisethermaldemagnetizationupto680°C
usingaMagneticMeasurementsThermalDemagnetiserSuperCooling(MMTDSC)furnaceoranASC–TD
48 furnace. Thermal demagnetization temperature intervals were 100–50°C below 550°C and shifted
to 30–10°C above 550°C. Remanent magnetization was measured using a 2G–755–4 K cryogenic
magnetometer.Theinstrumentsofmagnetometersanddemagnetizerswereinstalledwithinamagnetically
shieldedroomwithresidualfieldsoflessthan300nTatthePaleomagnetismandEnvironmentalMagnetism
Laboratory(PEML),ChinaUniversityofGeosciences,Beijing(CUGB).Characteristicremanentmagnetiza-
tion(ChRM) directionsweregained usingprincipalcomponentanalysis(Kirschvink, 1980)fromat least
foursuccessivethermaldemagnetizationsteps.SitemeandirectionswerecalculatedusingFisherianstatis-
tics (Fisher, 1953). Paleomagnetic data were analyzed using the published computer program packages
developedbyEnkin(1990)andCogné(2003).
3. RockMagnetic Results
3.1. AMSAnalysis
TheAMSwasmeasuredfor288specimensfromtheJingzhushanFormationredbeds(Figure3).Meanmag-
neticsusceptibility(K )fromnorthernandsouthernlimboffoldsis177×10
−6and186×10 −6SI(<500μ
m
SI),respectively.TherelativelyweakvaluesofK suggestthattheAMSisdominantlycontrolledbypara- m
magnetic minerals (mainly phyllosilicates) and antiferromagnetic minerals (mainly hematite) (Huang
etal.,2006;Weil&Yonkee,2009).

4. Paleomagnetic Results
Four hundred and fifty‐three specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal demagnetization. Typical

ponent(LTC)wasisolatedbelow300°C.ThemeandirectionfortheLTCisD ¼354.6°,I ¼49.0°,k¼18.8° g g

field. After the LTC was removed, a stable univectorial high‐temperature component (HTC) decaying
toward the origin could be isolated between 400°C and 660–680°C, and defines as the ChRM directions.

5. Discussion
EventhoughthesitemeandirectionoftheJingzhushanFormation
passes McElhinny (1964) fold test, the mean inclination calculated
from 31 paleomagnetic sites of the northern limb of folds
(I ¼19.0°)issignificantlylowerthanthatof23paleomagneticsites
s
ofthesouthernlimboffolds(I ¼51.8°)(Table1).Thislargediscre- s
pancyofthemeaninclinationofthetwolimbsoffoldsmaybeattrib-
Figure6.Equal‐areaprojectionsofthesitemeandirectionsoftheLTCfromthe
uted to several factors: (1) the depositional and/or compaction of
Gejiarea.
sedimentary rocks may cause the inclination shallowing (Ding
et al., 2015; Kodama, 2012; Tan et al., 2010; Tauxe & Kent, 2004);
(2)theoriginalstratawerenothorizontalbutinclinedwhenthesedimentaryrocksgotmagnetization,so
theinclinationobtainedfromthetwolimbsoffoldswasquitedifferent(Satoetal.,2011;Tongetal.,2019);
(3)thechemicalremanentmagnetization(CRM)wasacquiredafterdepositionoftheredbeds,whichcan
obscuretheprimarycomponent(Jiangetal.,2015;Kodama&Dekkers,2004);(4)theremanencedirections
obtainedfromthetwolimbsoffoldsmayhavebeeninfluencedbythedistortionalstrains(Cognéetal.,1991;
Kanamatsu & Herrero‐Bervera, 2006; Kligfield et al., 1983). The above four possibilities are discussed
separately.
5.1. CauseoftheInclinationDiscrepancy
5.1.1. InclinationShallowingCorrection
Previousstudiesindicatedthatlowerinclinationsobtainedfromsedimentaryrocksmayhavesufferedfrom
depositional and/or compaction‐induced inclination shallowing (Kodama, 2012; Tauxe & Kent, 2004).
Therefore, applicable correction methods such as the elongation/inclination (E/I) correction (Tauxe &
Kent,2004)andanisotropy‐basedinclinationshallowingcorrection(Hodych&Buchan,1994)arewidely
usedtotestwhethercompaction‐inducedinclinationshallowingissignificantinsedimentaryrocks(Tong
et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019). It is worth noting that the declinations of the northern limb of folds
(DZ1–27,andDZ51–54)showadifferenceof~11°withthatofthesouthernlimboffolds(DZ28–50),indicat-
ing that local vertical‐axis rotations may have occurred in the study area. Thus, in this study the
anisotropy‐based inclination shallowing correction method (Hodych & Buchan, 1994) was used to test
andcorrecttheextentofinclinationdeviation.
Atotalof14corespecimensfromsevenhandblocks,whichweredrilledperpendiculartothestratabedding
plane, were measured for anisotropy‐based inclination shallowing correction. The IRMx (IRM measured
paralleltothebedding)andIRMz(IRMmeasuredperpendiculartothebedding)forthe14corespecimens
were first acquired using an ASC IM10–30 pulse magnetizer at angle of 45° to the bedding and then
measuredusinga JR–6Aspinner magnetometer.When the IRMacquiredin1,000mT,stepwisethermal
demagnetizationwascarriedoutusinganMMTDSC.
Theresultsofthe14corespecimensareshowninTable2andFigure8.ThevaluesofIRMz/IRMxacquired
between200and1,000mTandthosebetween600°Cand680°Crangingfrom1.0705–0.9795and1.0640–
0.9686,respectively.Besides,themeanvaluesof IRMz/IRMx fromtwo limbsoffoldsareconsistentwith
eachother,andbotharecloseto1.Inthisstudy,themeanvalueofIRMz/IRMxinthethermaldemagnetiza-
tiontemperaturebetween600°Cand680°Cwasusedtocorrectthemeaninclination.Thecorrectedmean

5.1.4. RelationshipsBetweenRemanenceDirectionsand
DistortionalStrains
Foldingofrocksnotonlycausesthestratatotiltbutalsoproduces
obviously internal distortional strains within the rock layers; thus,
the distortional strains could affect the direction of remanence
(Graham, 1949; Kligfield et al., 1983). The relationship between
remanencedirectionsanddistortionalstrainshavebeenextensively
investigated by the use of the experimental simulation and AMS
(Blow&Hamilton,1978;Cognéetal.,1991;Gaoetal.,2014;Huang
etal.,2006;Kligfieldetal.,1983).Forexample,studiesoftherema-
nent magnetization of artificial redepositions of naturally
occurring deep sea sediments indicate that postdepositional
compactionisaprincipalfactorforinclinationshallowing(Blow&
Hamilton, 1978). Analysis of AMS and ChRM directions from
PermianredbedsintheAlpesMaritimes(France)indicatesthatinci-
pientdeformationandpencilstructuremagneticfabricinrockshave

5.2. TheShapeoftheAsianSouthernMarginPriortoIndia‐AsiaCollision
Consideringthat(1)theinclinationobtainedfrombothCretaceousvolcanicandsedimentaryrocksofthe
northern limb of folds are obviously lower than those from the southern limb, which may be related to
thesyntectonicsedimentation(Tongetal.,2019)and(2)thesignificantdifferencesofdeclinationsofthe
Cretaceous paleomagnetic data sets in the LT may be influenced by the regional vertical axis rotations
(Bianetal.,2017;Yang,Ma,Zhang,etal.,2015),weutilizethreeapproachestoconstrainthesouthernedge
ofAsiabeforeIndia‐Asiacollision.Thefirstapproachiscalledthesmallcirclefittingmethod,whichfollows
themethodofMardiaandGadsden(1977)withtheprocedureofCogné(2003)tocalculatethecolatitudeand
obtainthecorrespondingpaleolatitude.Thesecondapproachiscalledtheinclination‐onlymeanarithmetic
method,whichusesthemethodproposedbyDoubrovineandTarduno(2008)withtheproceduredesigned
byArasonandLevi(2010)tocalculatethemeaninclinationandobtainthecorrespondingpaleolatitude.The
third approach is called the syntectonic‐sedimentation‐correction method, which follows the method of
Tong et al. (2019) to first calculate the original dip of the syntectonic sedimentation (α) and then obtain
the tilt‐corrected site mean directions and its corresponding paleolatitude. Given that (1) the
anisotropy‐basedinclinationshallowingcorrectionofLateCretaceousJingzhushanFormationredbedsin
the Dingqing and Geji area of the LT showed that no compaction‐induced inclination shallowing has
occurred in redbeds (Tong etal., 2017; this study);(2) the consistent inclination recordedin Cretaceous
red beds and interbedded basalt flows indicated that no significant inclination shallowing resulted from
deposition compaction in red beds (Cao, Sun, Li, et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2006); (3) the
inclination‐only mean data from Cretaceous red beds and volcanic rocks in the LT showed that the
compaction‐inducedinclinationshallowingisnotsignificantinredbeds(Yang,Ma,Zhang,etal.,2015).
WeusedsedimentarypaleomagneticdataoftheLTwithoutinclinationshallowingcorrectioninthisstudy.
PublishedCretaceouspaleomagneticdatasetsfromtheLTarelistedinTable3andthewell‐acceptedseven
reliabilitycriteria(VanderVoo,1990)wereusedtoappraisethem.Becausethereliabilitycriteriaarestrict
andthereexistsalongCretaceousnormalsuperchron(~126–83.6Ma;Gradsteinetal.,2012),fewdatacan
meetallsevencriteria.Inthisstudy,wesuggestthatrobustpaleomagneticdatamustcontainatleastone
positivefieldtest(suchasfold,conglomerate,orcontacttest)orthepresenceofreversalsbesidestheother
fivereliabilitycriteria.
ForthewesternLT,atotalof12availableCretaceouspaleopoleshavebeenreported;theirpaleolatitudes
havebeencalculatedforthereferencepoint(32.7°N,81.4°E)inourstudyarea.Amongthem,onepaleopole
(CY)isfromonlythreesites(22specimens)andlackarobustfieldtest.Wethusdonotusethispaleopolefor
furtheranalyses.Theremaining11paleopoles,whichfulfilledourreliabilitycriteria,areindistinguishable
within95%confidencelimitsandalignonasmallcirclecenteredonthereferencepoint(32.7°N,81.4°E)
(Figure 11a). First, we used the small circle fitting method to calculate the colatitude and then obtained
thecorrespondingpaleolatitude.Thefittedsmallcirclepassesthroughthe11selectedpaleopolesandgives
a colatitude of 72.5° ± 2.3°N. This indicates that the western LT was located at the paleolatitude of
17.5° ± 2.3°N for the reference point (32.7°N, 81.4°E) (Figure 11a and Table 3). Second, we used the
inclination‐onlymean arithmeticmethodtocalculatethe meaninclination andthen obtainedthe corre-
spondingpaleolatitude.Atotalof281Cretaceouspaleomagneticsites(2,549specimens)fromthewestern

Figure 12.Paleolatitude plots for the Lhasa terrane. The shaded areas and vertical bars show the errors of the paleolatitudes. Expected and observed
paleolatitudesofthewesternLTwerecalculatedusingthereferencepoint(32.7°N,81.4°E)inourstudyarea,andthereferencepoint(32.7°N,91.1°E)forthe
centraleasternLT.
Therefore, we first use the small circle fitting method to calculate the colatitude and then obtain the
correspondingpaleolatitude.Thefittedsmallcirclepassesthroughthe10selectedpaleopolesandgivesa
colatitude of 73.2°± 3.6°N. This indicatesthat the central‐eastern LT waslocated atthe paleolatitudeof
16.8° ± 3.6°N for the reference point (32.7°N, 91.1°E) (Figure 11c and Table 3). Then we used the
inclination‐only mean arithmetic method to calculate the mean inclination and obtained the
corresponding paleolatitude. A total of 168 Cretaceous paleomagnetic sites (1,325 specimens) from the
central eastern LT give an inclination‐only mean of 30.6° ± 2.1° and a corresponding paleolatitude of
16.5°±1.3°N(Table3andTableS3inthesupportinginformation).
Althoughthe10CretaceouspaleopolesfromthecentraleasternLTfulfilledourreliabilitycriteria,onlyone
paleomagneticdataset fromthe two limbsof folds(Sunetal.,2012).The paleomagneticdata setofSun
et al. (2012) after syntectonic‐sedimentation correction yielded paleolatitudes of 19.1° ± 4.9°N and
17.0°±16.7°Nforthesouthernandnorthernlimboffoldsforthereferencepoint(32.7°N,91.1°E),respec-
tively. Given that (1) the results of the central‐eastern LT obtained from the syntectonic‐sedimentation‐
correction method (17.0–19.1°) are generally consistent with the results of small circle fitting method
(16.8°±3.6°N)andinclination‐onlymeanarithmeticmethod(16.5°±1.3°N);(2)onlyonepaleomagnetic
resultisobtainedfromthetwolimbsoffolds,andtheresultofthenorthernlimboffoldshasawideerror
range(17.0°±16.7°N)becauseitwasobtainedfromonlythreepaleomagneticsites;(3)theresultsofthese
threemethodsofthewesternLTareindistinguishablewitheachother;(4)therearemultiplesolutionsfor
the syntectonic‐sedimentation correction with other paleomagnetic data in the central eastern LT (Tong
etal.,2019),weusedthepaleolatitudeobtainedfromthesmallcirclefittingmethodastheprecollisional
paleogeography of the central eastern LT. Obviously, for the same reference latitude of 32.7°N, the
Cretaceouspaleolatitudeof17.5°±2.3°NobtainedfromthewesternLTisconsistentwiththeCretaceous
paleolatitudeof 16.8° ±3.6°N yieldedfromthe centraleastern LT,revealingthat the shape of the Asian
southern margin is generally similar to its present‐day relatively east‐west alignment prior to India‐Asia
collision(Figures1aand12).

6. Conclusions
WepresentnewpaleomagneticresultsfromtheJingzhushanFormationredbedsinthewesternLT.Our
newpaleomagneticresults,combinedwiththereliableCretaceouspaleomagneticresultsfromtheLT,allow
ustoreachthefollowingconclusions:
1. Thetilt‐correctedsitemeandirectionfor54sitesisD ¼10.2°,I ¼33.1°,k ¼17.2,α ¼4.8°,corre-
s s s 95
spondingtoapalaeopoleat74.4°N,226.0°EwithA ¼3.8°.Thispaleomagneticdatasetpassespositive
95
foldtestsandindicatesthatthestudiedareawaslocatedat19.6°±3.8°NduringtheLateCretaceous.
2. The influence of the distortional strains on remanence directions or depositional and/or
compaction‐inducedinclinationshallowingoftheJingzhushanFormationredbedsintheGejiareaof
thewesternLTcanbeignored.
3. TheJingzhushanFormationredbedsintheGejiarearecordaprimarydetritalhematiteorigin.
4. TheinclinationobtainedfromtheJingzhushanFormationredbedsintheGejiareamayinfluencedby
thesyntectonicsedimentation.Notably,thesitemeandirectionisgenerallyconsistentwiththesitemean
direction obtained after syntectonic‐sedimentation correction; However, the site mean direction will
haveawideinfluencerangeifthepaleomagneticdataareobtainedfromonlyonelimboffoldsintheuni-
dentifiedsyntectonicgrowthstrata.
5. The Cretaceous paleolatitude of the LT obtained by three methods (small circle fitting method,
inclination‐onlymeanarithmeticmethod, andsyntectonic‐sedimentation‐correctionmethod)is indis-
tinguishablewitheachother,indicatingthatthesouthernmarginofAsiahadapresent‐dayrelatively
east‐westalignmentpriortoIndia‐Asiacollision.
